title: Congo Forest Intelligence: Connecting Forest Evidence to Finance and Community Results
summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo already has forest monitoring and environmental-finance systems. Congo Forest Intelligence (CFI) is a proposed, unbuilt integration pilot to test whether linking existing observations, public commitments, financing and locally verified results can improve traceability without duplicating these systems.

blocks.text: Key findings

items.text: In the Congo Basin, annual humid tropical primary forest loss increased from 0.38% of baseline area in 2023 to 0.44% in 2024, a rise of 0.06 percentage points. This is a regional measure, not a CFI effect. WRI analysis.

blocks.text: Context

At COP31 in Antalya, the Presidency advocated stronger payment for tropical-forest ecosystem services and highlighted the proposed Kivu-Kinshasa Green Corridor. The Presidency described the corridor as covering more than 540,000 km². That is a policy-reported initiative footprint, not an independently audited number of hectares already protected or a measured outcome. Presidency, 11 November; Presidency, 10 November.

blocks.text: Remaining gaps or unmet needs

The candidate gap is not missing satellite data. It is whether analysts can consistently connect a named commitment to its geographic scope, a dated funding record, an implementation milestone and an independently checked environmental or community outcome. Public evidence of a general, nationwide failure to do this has not been established. The proposed gap must be validated for a specific program and user workflow before committing to software.

FAO documented continuing work on standardizing methods, coordinating institutions and strengthening sustainable management of DRC forest data in November 2026. This supports further investigation of integration needs, but does not prove the CFI design is superior. FAO findings.

blocks.text: What YNK Tech adds

Proposed CFI minimum viable scope: (1) a source-linked register of 20 to 40 publicly documented commitments in one selected geography, (2) permitted references to forest change and relevant project boundaries, (3) a dated financing and milestone ledger, and (4) a reviewable outcome record with uncertainty and local-consent controls. The pilot would surface missing records, conflicting dates and unverifiable claims instead of filling gaps with AI-generated certainty.

Every record should distinguish announcement, contract, disbursement, activity and observed outcome. Geospatial data should be used to trigger inquiry, not to infer illegality, ownership, additionality or community consent. AI assistance could support document matching and draft explanations only under human review.
Build, partner or integrate?

Integration-first is the recommended path. Use GNW/GFW observations under appropriate licenses; align with DIAF and the national system; reference CAFI or other official finance records instead of scraping or claiming ownership; and invite Congolese researchers and community representatives to validate indicators and consent rules. A custom product is justified only if a comparative pilot demonstrates decision value beyond these incumbents.

A no-build result is acceptable. If the sampled users already obtain complete, timely and trustworthy evidence from current tools, YNK Tech should document that finding and propose training, integration guidance or independent evaluation rather than another platform.

Proposed implementation roadmap and safeguards

items: Days 1-30: select one legally appropriate pilot area and two incumbent workflows; inventory accessible source datasets, coverage, licenses, boundaries, and consent needs; define the same 40-case sample and independent reviewers.

Days 31-60: build only a read-only, versioned evidence register and comparison interface; reconcile identities, dates, funding milestones and source citations; conduct privacy, data quality and security review.
Days 61-90: run blinded side-by-side evaluations, verify errors with Congolese subject-matter experts, publish both favorable and unfavorable pilot findings, and decide to partner, refine or stop.

blocks.text: Safeguards must include source provenance and corrections, separate observed/estimated/official statuses, access restrictions for sensitive community details, non-discriminatory interpretation, independent methodological review, licensing checks, clear institutional roles and transparent cost reporting. Do not create a public list of sensitive community locations or infer legal responsibility from a satellite alert.
What to watch next
Next evidence checkpoints, independent of whether CFI proceeds:

items: Within 30 days: verify Green Corridor legal boundaries and available project-level financing disclosures, rather than reusing broad political area figures as implementation progress.
Within 60 days: seek documentation of existing national and CAFI reporting coverage, retention rules and publicly available outcome verification.
Within 90 days: if authorized, perform the side-by-side pilot and publish comparator metrics, errors, costs and a go/no-go decision.

blocks.text: Methodology and limitations

This study uses official DRC communications as evidence of announced priorities, WRI as a source of published forest-loss estimates, FAO/GFOI as evidence about existing national monitoring and CAFI as evidence about its operating finance and PES tools. No source establishes that CFI is developed, endorsed, funded or operational. Presidency; WRI; FAO; CAFI.

blocks.text: Forest-loss rates are definitions-specific and cannot be equated with permanent deforestation, avoided emissions, project impact, protected hectares or financing results. WRI year-to-year comparisons may change with updated classifications or methods. The 2024 six-country rates are not interchangeable with DRC-only 2025 figures. Pilot scenarios illustrate arithmetic only; no causal or financial effect is claimed.
